INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to submit on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred Forty Second Report on Functioning of Private Airports and related
issues.
2. The Government of India had decided to modernize and upgrade the existing domestic and
international airports at Mumbai and Delhi to world standards and to construct Greenfield airports
in Bangalore and Hyderabad through Public Private Partnership. The Greenfield airports in
Hyderabad and Bangalore have started functioning from the 23rd March and 24th May, 2008
respectively. The modernization of Delhi and Mumbai Airports are in different stages of
development.
3. There were a large number of reports/representations about the problems faced by the
passengers and associated agencies at Mumbai and Delhi Airports and also at Bengaluru and
Hyderabad after the new Greenfield airports were opened and the old ones were closed. The
Committee while discussing these issues felt it necessary to visit these airports for an on-the-
spot assessment of the problems and to see facilities available at these airports. Accordingly,
the Committee visited the new airports at Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Mumbai from the 14th to
20th September, 2008 on this issue. The Committee also visited the old airport at Begumpet, in
Hyderabad. The Committee had already visited the Delhi Airport on l0th January, 2008. The
Committee interacted with various stakeholders at these airports for finalizing its report.
4. Apart from passenger amenities, the Committee has also dealt with various issues/points
relating to the policy of privatization of airports, procedures adopted for this and other related
matters.
5. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the representatives of the Ministry of Civil
Aviation, Airports Authority of India, managements of Bangalore International Airport Ltd. (BIAL),
Hyderabad International Airport Ltd. (HIAL), Mumbai International Airport Ltd. (MIAL) and Delhi
International Airport Ltd. (DIAL) for placing before the Committee the material and information
desired in connection with the subject and for clarifying the points raised by the Members.
6. The committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the
20th October, 2008.
SITARAM YECHURY
N
EW D ELHI; Chairman,
October 20, 2008 Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Asvina 28, 1930  (Saka) Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture.

1
REPORT
India is experiencing a phenomenal growth in its aviation sector which plays a vital role in
the overall economic growth of the country. The Indian civil aviation sector has shown an
extraordinary growth rate in the last few years. In 2006-07, total air passenger traffic increased
by 32.6% with around 78.7 million passengers, of whom 57.5 million reflecting an increase of
40.5% were domestic passengers and 21.2 million showing an increase of 15% in international
sector. Present slackness in aviation sector both national and international, notwithstanding, the air
passenger traffic is expected to grow in the coming years.
2. Presently, India has a total of 454 airports or airstrips including operational, non-operational,
abandoned and unused airports, of which 138 belong to India’s defence establishment, 97 to
Airports Authority of India (AAI), 158 to various State Governments, and 61 to its fledgling private
sector. Due to increase in traffic both domestic and international, movement of aircrafts has also
gone up rapidly. However, such a growth in air traffic has led to strain on the available aviation
infrastructure, which is already over-stretched. It has resulted in traffic congestions and delays
mainly at the major airports. To sustain this boom in the civil aviation sector, an urgent need for
expansion and improvement of the airport infrastructure was felt to cope up with the emerging
requirements. Airports being the centres of economic activity, play a crucial role in the Nation’s
economy. Faced with. such a situation, the Government is working on a proposal of getting around
500 airports operational by 2020, which would include redevelopment of currently unused airports,
Greenfield airports, and also ‘merchant’ airports dedicated to the movement of cargo and logistics.
It is estimated that by 2020, Indian airports should be able to handle 100 million passengers
including 60 million domestic passengers and cargo in the range of 3.4 million tones per annum.
3. The Government decided to modernize and upgrade some for the existing domestic and
international airports to world standards. The Government through its Airport Infrastructure Policy
of 1997, decided to set up Greenfield Airports in the country. As a result, permission was granted
to construct two Greenfield Airports at Devanahalli in Bengaluru and Shamshabad in Hyderabad on
joint venture basis in PPP mode. The selected companies, namely, GMR Hyderabad International
Airport Ltd. (GHIAL); and Bengaluru International Airport Ltd. (BIAL) entered into Concession
Agreements separately with the Government of India for development, construction operation and
maintenance of the Airports at these places. Both these airports have started functioning from 2008.
The Government also handed over the Delhi and Mumbai airports to the Joint Venture Companies
namely, GMR and GVK groups respectively for modernization. The modernization of these airports
is in different stages of development.
4. There were a large number of reports/representations about the problems faced by the
passengers and associated agencies at Mumbai and Delhi Airports and also at Bengaluru and
Hyderabad after the new Greenfield airports were opened and the old ones were closed. The
Committee while discussing these Issues felt it necessary to visit these private airports for an on-
the-spot assessment of the problems and to see facilities available at these airports.
5. The Committee, accordingly, visited new airports at Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Mumbai
from the 14th to 20th September, 2008. The Committee also visited the old Begumpet airport at
Hyderabad. The Committee had taken stock of the facilities, available and proposed, as also the
problems being faced by the passengers/tourist, Airports Authority of India (AAI), Private Airline
operators and other associated agencies at these airports. The Committee also discussed the issues
at length with the representatives of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, Airports Authority of India,
CEOs of BIAL, HIAL and MIAL, Airports Authority Employees Unions and Private Airlines.

2
Operators. During its visit, the Committee had also received a large number of written
representations from various stakeholders.
(A) Bengaluru International Airport Limited (BIAL)
6. The Committee has been informed that the BIAL is being developed to handle upto 11
million passengers as Greenfield airport at Devanahalli near Bengaluru on a Build Operate and
Transfer (BOT) basis with Public Private Participation. Government of Karnataka through Karnataka
State Industrial Investment Development Corporation (KSIIDC) and AAI each hold 13% equity and
the strategic joint venture partners hold the balance 74%. A Memorandum of Understandlng to this
effect was signed on the 3rd May 1999, between AAI and KSIIDC to facilitate further action
leading to implementation of the project.
7. A consortium led by Siemens, Germany with Unique Zurich, Switzerland and Larsen and
Toubro India Ltd. as other members, have been chosen as the strategic Joint Venture Partners.
Government of Karnataka is extending Rs.3.5 billon as State support and is providing approximately
4000 acres of land on concessional rate. AAI’s investment in the equity is capped at Rs. 50 crore,
while the approximate cost of the project is Rs. 1400 crore.
8. While the construction of the new airport commenced on the 2nd July, 2005, it started its
operations from the 24th May; 2008.
9. During the course of discussions, the representatives of BIAL informed the Committee that
the project implementation of BIAL has been done with thrust on predominant use of locally
available input materials. Meticulous supervision and stringent quality control were enforced during
project implementation. In the Phase-I of the Project Implementation, BIAL has constructed the
following facilities:
(a) Operational Facilities: This airport currently has Runway which is 4000 mts. long and 60 mts.
wide with 6 exits. It has 9 Aerobridges, 8 one armed and 1 double armed. There are 42 Aircrafts
stands (Code C aircraft stands). It provides 13 Security counters (8 Domestic and 5 International)
and has five level security screening system for checked-in baggage. Immigration Counters are 18,
both departure and arrival. It has a Cargo Capacity of 350,000 tons annually (presently
160,000.tons).
(b) Terminal building Facilities: This airport has 53 check-in counters including 18 self check-
in counters. It has single check-in process with no queues for screening baggage. Various facilities
like Valet Service, Shops, restaurants and lounges (common & dedicated), Short walkways, Baby
care, 24 hour pharmacy, Special needs-elevators with Braille Plates and Free Wi-Fi access have also
been provided at this airport.
Buses: 46 V ayu Vajra AC V olvo buses and 23 Suvara non AC buses are run for airport shuttle
service having minimum fare of Rs.70 and Maximum of Rs.200 for AC buses and Rs.20 to 90 for
non-AC buses.
Taxi: AC Taxi Services- Merucabs and Easycabs, equipped with tracking service are also being run.
Post paid taxis are available on meter charges @Rs.15/-per km. Cars can be rented for self drive-
a new concept at an Indian airport
Car parking arrangements: Airport has a car parking with 2000 car park slots, in which 700
car park slots are for employees. Charges are: for the first 10 minutes free, Rs.40/- for 2 hours
and Rs.20 per additional hour, Rs.300 for 24 hrs with Rs.200 for every additional day. Porter
services are there for minimum Rs.70 for up to 3 bags and V alet service is for Rs.150.
Helicopter: Deccan Aviations helicopter shuttle service has provided 3 pick up points - Electronic
city, Whitefield, Palace grounds and HAL, operating between 630 hours to 1800 hours. Minimum

3
fare is Rs.4800/- and maximum fare is Rs.5800/- per person per trip. New Service by Global
Vectra heli services will begin in October, 2008.
Travel retail unlocked
• Airport has a design reflecting the flowers of Lal Bagh. It has a mix of domestic and
international brands in 18 shopping outlets to choose from. It has Duty Free Shops at
arrival and departure areas and 15 Food and Beverages outlets ranging from local cuisine
to international cafes. It has 2 Lounges and another 2 more in the making. Additional
reserved lounge are being created.
• It had handled 2.5 million passengers as on August 29, 2008, with 30,000 air craft
movements and 45,000 MT of cargo. It has seen 30% increase in international flights.
BIAL has approx.5000 employees.
• It claimed 70% increase in the toilets and increase in passenger seating areas and seats
and has installed drinking water fountains.
• It handled on an average 151 arrival/departure flights per day with departure of 9431
domestic passengers and departure of 2283 international passengers per day.
• Average arrival of domestic passengers per day is 9330 and of international passengers
per day was 2279.
Extension Plan
Phase – 1:  The BIAL extension plan has been design to expand and upgrade infrastructure of the
Initial Project, Re-design 2006, Trumpet Fly-over, Airline Buildings, Greenery and canopy and
Security Equipment PSF.
Phase – 2:  This phase is the implementation of several immediate measures such as Apron
Expansion and Express Terminal
Phase – 3:  Phase 3 to be completed by 2012 includes Terminal 2 and Second runway
(B) Hyderabad International Airport Limited (HIAL)
10. HIAL also is a public-private joint venture between GMR Group, Malaysia Airports Holdings
Berhad and the State Government of Andhra Pradesh and Airports Authority of India (AAI). The
Greenfield airport at Shamshabad near Hyderabad is being implemented on a Build Operate and
Transfer (BOT) basis with Public Private Participation. The Government of Andhra Pradesh (GoAP)
have selected a consortium led by M/s GMR as the developer for this airport. The Government
of Andhra Pradesh and AAI together hold 26% equity, with AAI’s investment in the equity capped
at Rs.50 crore. The joint venture partners, GMR Group holds the balance 74% in the Company
namely, Hyderabad International Airport Ltd. (HIAL) set up to implement the project. The
Government of Andhra, Pradesh extended Rs.315 crore as State support and Rs.107 crore as, a
grant. Further, Government of Andhra Pradesh provided 5000 acres of land on concessional rate.
The concession Agreement between the GoI and HIAL was executed on the 20th December 2004.
11. The Committee visited the Shamshabad airport on the 17th September, 2008 and was
informed that the total project cost, as per the DPR submitted by HIAL, was estimated to be
Rs.I400 crore (2005 figure). This was being financed by State support to the extent of
Rs.422 crore and rest by way of Debt and Equity to the tune of 40% and 60%, respectively. This
project cost was for estimated passenger traffic of 5 million. However, the final cost of the project
is Rs.2920 crore for estimated passenger traffic of 12 million. The new airport started its
operations from the 23rd March, 2008.

4
12. During the course of the discussion with the Committee, the representative of HIAL
presented the following facts about the passenger amenities available at the airport:
Location: Airport is located at 25Km/I9 miles from Begumpet, the old airport. It is operating 22
airlines connecting 35 destinations which is further growing. Total area of the project is 5495
acres.
Airport Capacity:  It has initial passenger capacity of 12 million persons per annum (MPPA), with
the ultimate capacity of over 40, MPPA. Initial car go capacity is l 1akh MT/Per Annum (MTPA)
and final capacity would be 1.3 million, MTPA. It has an exclusive cargo apron for four, code C
freighter aircraft with facility for “Express/Courier’ cargo.
Operational facilities: It has India’s longest runway (4.2 km) which is A 380 Compatible and has
India’s longest taxiway (4.2 km). Airport has 10 runway entry/exit points (including four rapid exit
taxiways).
Car Parking arrangements:  It has parking area for 3000 cars in front of passenger terminal
building providing easy Transit from domestic to international and vice-versa.
Terminal building facilities: It has 130 Check-in-counters with CUTE (Common User Terminal
Equipment) and 16 self check-in kiosks with CUSS (Common User Self Service).
• 46 Immigration counters - 23 departure and 22 arrival and 1 transit. . City Check-in
facility has been proposed at Begumpet and Secunderabad Railway Stations. There are
42 aircraft parking stands including 12 passenger boarding bridges.
• It uses modem IT systems like FIDS (Flight Information Display Systems), ACN
(Airport Community Network), Baggage Tag & Boarding Card Printers etc. It claimed
to have tallest A TC Tower (75 mtr.).
• The Committee was informed that the Airport has a full fledged medical center,
international brand concessionaires, radio taxis system and Aero express shuttle services.
A business hotel with 308 rooms is also coming up.
• For security, 4 level in-line baggage security system has been put in place with
perimeter intrusion detection system.
• The airport had completed 178 days of operation and handled 3.10 million passengers,
with average daily ATMs of 240. it also claimed that ATF Sales had increased from 550
KL/day as compared to old Begumpet airport to around 880 KL/day now.
• GMR management claimed to have taken feedback/suggestions from 1.5 lakh passengers
and other stakeholders till date and had incorporated these inputs to improve the
services further and increase passenger convenience.
13. The Committee found the plan and design of the Greenfield airports to be of the
international standard with certain useful facilities for the comfort and convenience of the
passengers, for example, adequate and efficient check-in counters, self check-in machines
and quick immigration clearance, large number of shops, eateries, etc. However, the
Committee also came across certain areas that needed immediate attention. For example,
the Committee found that the passengers at the Greenfield airports have to pay exorbitant
prices for food items. The eateries are charging much more than the MRP, which is against
the Supreme Court order. There is no separate canteen for the employees and the staff
working at the airports. The drivers and others who are waiting outside the airports have
no affordable canteen facility and basic amenities like toilets and bathrooms. The
Committee recommends that the Government should ensure that the Greenfield Airports at

5
Bengaluru and Hyderabad provide basic facilities to the drivers and passengers and stop the
eateries from charging exorbitant prices. Private airlines have to cough up hefty amounts
for parking bays and aerobridges, security charges, lounge rentals, telephone rentals and
other facilities at the new airports.
14. The parking charges for vehicles are also quite heavy at the new airports. At
Bengaluru, it is Rs.40/- per hour and Rs.20/-per additional hours. The Committee is
surprised to know that at Hyderabad airport, a vehicle while entering the airport for
dropping or picking up a passenger has to pay Rs.35/- per trip. The Committee notes that
space earmarked for passenger seating areas was inadequate and numbers of seats are also
not adequate, causing inconvenience to the passengers during peak times. This is so because
much of the airport space has been let out for commercial use and given to shopping outlets
and F&B outlets. There is conspicuous absence of lounges at these airports. There is a need
for creation of additional reserved lounge for VIPs and passengers. To help and guide the
passengers at these airports, there should be round-the-clock help service at these airports.
There were inadequate facilities provided for free drinking water at these airports. More
drinking water fountains should be installed. The emergency medical facilities for treatment
of the passengers in case of sudden illness should be in place in all the new airports as has
been done at the new Hyderabad airport.
15. The Committee recommends that the flight delay or cancellation must be reported
to passengers well in time to avoid hardships to the passengers. The baggage handling
process should be strengthened so as to reduce the baggage delivery time and hardship to
the passengers. Apron driving discipline should be maintained to avoid any accident on
apron and staff should be given proper training for the driving skills and behaviours. There
should be integration of air and ground surveillance information along with flight related
data to enhance air. travel safety and efficient air traffic management.
16. The private operators should recognize various staff welfare committees of Airports
Authority of India and others working at these airports. There should be regular
consultative and coordination meeting of all the stakeholders at the new airports so as to
resolve the different issues/grievances.
17. The Committee learnt that it was discouraging for the short-haul passengers to take
air travel after the new airports. A higher User Development Fee (UDF) was being charged
by the new airport developers from the passengers. The user development fee added with
high taxi/bus fares due to long distances, compel the passengers to use other means of
transport such as road and trains for the short distance destinations. This has, in fact
rendered the air travel from these airports added with high ATF prices, just prohibitive.
18. The Committee notes that the Task force on Financing Plan for airports (July 2006)
had recommended that the users should not be burdened with ADF/UDF for financing at the
airport projects. This is particularly important in the context of the policy objective to make
civil aviation a mass, rather than an elitist model of travel and to make air travel more
affordable. After taking into account various aspects and the above recommendation of the
Task Force the committee feels that the imposition of UDF on passengers is a retrograde
step contravening the Task Force recommendations and recommends that the UDF imposed
on passengers may be withdrawn immediately and no more UDF may be imposed on
passengers in any of the airports.
19. CAPACITY OF BIAL AIRPORT
19.1 As per the original Concession Agreement (CA) dated 05.07.2004, BIAL was supposed to

6
build a Terminal of 55,000 sq. mtr. to accommodate 2017 passengers in the peak hour. This works
out to annual capacity of around 4.00 million passengers. The Committee was informed that the
CA was amended in 2006 and the capacity of the airport was enhanced to 2733 passengers during
peak hour with a terminal capacity of 71500 sq. m.
19.2 However, the current terminal is of total 71310 sq. m., out of which the basement area
consists of around 18665 sq. m. The basement area is neither used, nor usable by the passengers.
This space is used for storage, services and utilities. Hence, this cannot be counted while
computing the total terminal area. Also the kerb area of 5616 sq m outside the terminal which is
not a part of the terminal building and not used by passengers.
19.3 As per the IATA guidelines, the type of airport (level C) the area per peak hour passenger
(PHP) should be 26 sq m per passenger. As per the Concession Agreement, the area per passenger
should be 27.3 sq m. Hence, considering the actual terminal area available for passengers, the
capacity of the terminal works out to be 1928 PHP only, against the 2733 PHP capacity to be
provided as per the Concession Agreement.
19.4 As per the IATA standards, the area required for 10 million passengers per annum is 150000
sq. m. In view of the above, it can be inferred that the actual capacity of the BIAL terminal
building is still around 3.5 million only (1928 passengers per peak hour), which is much below the
capacity to be provided by BIAL as per the Concession Agreement.
19.5 BIAL was obligated to provide the facilities as per the IATA/ICAO standards. As per the
IATA standards the maximum commercial area permissible in the. terminal area is 12% of the total
passenger area. But in case of BIAL, 30% of terminal space has been utilised for commercial area.
If this aspect is considered the capacity of the terminal would further come down.
19.6 The Committee notes that the Government of India appears to be unconcerned about
the obligation of BIAL to construct and provide an airport as per the concession agreement.
Even the area and capacity were not verified before permitting to open new and closing HAL
Airport. This appears to be an irregularity committed by Government of India in this
matter.
20. During the meeting at Hyderabad the representatives of the AAEU argued that the idea
behind developing the Greenfield Airport was to handle the excess traffic beyond the capacity of
existing Airports. But, in this case, the entire commercial operations were diverted and old airport
was closed for commercial operation. This has deprived Airports Authority of India a huge revenue.
The Committee was informed that Begumpet Airport is having the full fledged infrastructure for
efficient operation of NTR Domestic Terminal/Rajiv Gandhi International Terminal. This airport has
handled wide bodied aircrafts defence/commercial/cargo airlines of various countries. Recently AAI
have spent roughly Rs.200 crore towards development of infrastructure of Begumpet Airport with
a commitment to serve to the public for another fifteen years. Presently the entire establishment
worth thousands of crores is lying idle.
21. Before commissioning of the Greenfield Airport, the airport at Hyderabad was the sixth
largest airport in India having 250 scheduled aircraft movements per day. 10 domestic and 13
international operators operated from this Airport. In 2006-07, a total of 69727 aircraft movement
was registered with the 5.87 millions passengers. In 2007-08, a total of 86484 aircrafts movements
were registered with 7.05 millions passengers. After commissioning of the new airports the old
airport is catering only to VVIP aircrafts, defence movement, local flying club, and movement
related to emergencies and general aviation including chartered aircrafts.
22. The Committee wanted to know the details of flights which were handled at old Hyderabad
Airport after its closure for commercial operations and RNFC collected by the Airports Authority

7
of India. The Committee was informed that a total number of 631 movements of Airforce Aircrafts
and 654 take off was done since the closure of airport till 5th July, 2008. As regard total number
of movement of private, non-commercial, non-revenue and VIP flights including helicopters was
478 landings and 479 take offs upto 5th September, 2008. The RNFC collected for casual flight
operations since March, 2008 is Rs.1,72,498.00. The Committee was informed that the short haul
traffic growth has been reduced after the opening of the new airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad.
The Aircraft movements per day from HAL Airport as on 23.05.08 were 361 whereas the aircraft
movement per day from HIAL as on 1st week of September, 2008 was 280.
23. It was also submitted before the Committee that Airports Authority of India with
comprehensive traffic study/survey can distribute the traffic for both the Airports on competitive
basis based on the handling capacity, peak load traffic on operative measurement basis with the
available infrastructure from the existing operating airport (Begumpet) comparing with Shamshabad
Airport, since the funnel point for both the airports are same with regard to traffic movement.
After commissioning the new Greenfield Airport by the private operator the practical difficulties for
the passengers and airline operators have increased enormously on various account such as road
travel, UDF, etc. which affects the air travelers very badly and the very purpose of low cost
airlines will be defeated. Therefore, the decision to close down the existing airport within the
frame-work of concession agreement needs to be reviewed immediately.
24. The Committee notes that hundreds of crores of rupees were spent for developing
infrastructure at the old airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad but it is lying unutilized due
to the closure of airports for commercial purposes. Another interesting thing brought to the
notice of the Committee is that the old airports, the HAL Airport and Begumpet airport,
are being used for operation of VIP flights, Non-schedule Flights, General Aviation,
Helicopter-Taxis, etc. During the deliberations of the Committee the Airports Authority of
India reported that there is absolutely no problem in opening up two airports
simultaneously in a city. The Committee therefore, recommends that the old airports of
Hyderabad and Bengaluru may be used exclusively for short haul flights which are operating
from the nearby airports.
25. The Committee also notes that the closure of HAL airport led to loss of jobs due to
reduction of flights and due to closure of airlines operators. Thousands of direct and indirect
workers also lost their jobs, this also includes trolley retrievers, small time vendors, taxi
drivers, auto drivers, loaders etc. Despite the assurances given by the BIAL and HIAL
managements, they have not been accommodated in the new airports. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that all those people who are directly or indirectly affected due to
closure of the HAL Airport and Begumpet Airport may be given preference and suitably
accommodated at the new Green Field Airports.
26. The Committee is of the opinion that the HAL Airport is most convenient for
common public due to it being situated closer to the City Centre, easy accessibility and
availability of multi-mode transport options like Bus, Auto, Taxis, even 2-wheeler, etc. HAL
Airport, therefore, would be more convenient and economical for public compared to BIAL
due to absence of UDF and less transportation cost due to multiple modes and shorter
distance. Less time in coming and going from the airport is also important aspect in this
regard.
27. The Committee further recommends that the old airports may be made operational
for short-haul passengers. Moreover, this is the practice being followed in many of the
major cities in the world wherein more than one airport exists. There is no reason or
justification for keeping the hundreds of crores of worth infrastructure at the old airports
idle just to be used for VIP and other flights.

CLOSURE OF HAL AND BEGUMPET AIRPORTS - SOME LEGAL AND PROCEDURAL ISSUES
28. During the visit of the Committee, there were wide ranging discussions with various
stakeholders of the Airports in Bengaluru and Hyderabad. The representatives of the Airports
Authority Employees Union gave a detailed presentation before the Committee inter alia on the legal
and procedural issues involved in the closure of HAL Airport at Bengaluru and Begumpet Airport
at Hyderabad.
29. During the discussion at Bangaluru, the representatives of the Airports Authority Employees
Union (AAEU) submitted before the Committee that the Government was adopting a strange policy
of privatising and closing down the profit-making airports of Airports Authority of India; AAI was
struggling to manage to cross-subsidise non-profit making airports in the remote areas, from the
revenue it was earning through the profit-making airports. The Committee was informed that during
2004, Prime Minister of India had formed a Tripartite Committee to look into various issues
connected with airport infrastructure. The Chairman of the Tripartite Committee had given
categorical assurance to the Joint Forum and to AAEU on 13.10.06 that even after the opening of
BIAL Airport, HAL Airport will be functioning and airlines will be given the freedom to choose
between the two airports.
30. AAEU have also brought before the Committee various facts and arguments in connection
with the closure of HAL Airport, Bengaluru. Various points raised by Airports Authority of India
Employees Union were forwarded by the Committee to the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 3rd
October, 2008 for their comments. Even after reminders the Ministry did not offer their comments
till the writing of this Report.
31. Some of the major issues submitted before the Committee by them during the deliberations
are given are in the following paragraphs:
31.1 No comprehensive Privatisation Policy for the airports
31.1.1 It was argued that in the post-liberalisation era, privatisation had been done in sectors in
which only public sector organisations were present like Airlines, Insurance, Banking, Petroleum
etc.: In all these above sectors, not even a branch of any PSUs were closed down after private
players entered and a healthy competition was allowed between them resulting in quality services
at much competitive price. Also, the total volume of business in all these sectors also increased
due to competition. The Government, however, has signed an agreement with BIAL to close down
HAL Airport owned by AAI for commercial operations. This action of GoI is not at all consistent
with its own policy in other sectors.
31.2 Violation of 150 Km. norm
31.2.1 The Committee was informed that in 1997, Government of India announced a policy on
airport infrastructure which said that no Greenfield airport will normally be allowed within an aerial
distance of 150 kilometers of an existing airport. Where it is allowed as a second airport in the
same city or close vicinity, the parameters for distribution of traffic between the two airports will
be clearly spelt out. But the Bengaluru and Hyderabad Greenfield airports were permitted within 150
kms of radius of the existing airports in violation of the said policy. Also, the distribution of the
traffic between the two airports was also not spelt out.
31.2.2 It was further contended that as per this “a Greenfield airport may be permitted where an
existing airport is unable to meet the projected requirements of traffic or a new focal point of
traffic emerges with sufficient viability. It can be allowed both as a replacement for an existing
airport or for simultaneous operation. This aspect will have to be clearly spelt out in the notice

9
inviting tenders.” Therefore, this fact ought to have been clearly spelt out in the notice inviting
tender in the case of Bengaluru and Hyderabad. But the notice inviting tender did not contain any
clause about closure of HAL Airport.
31.3 Airports Authority Act, 1994
31.3.1 It was further contended that there was no provision in the AAI Act 1994, to close down
an AAI airport, particularly, ‘only for commercial purposes’. The representatives of AAEU further
submitted that an MoU signed between AAI and Karnataka Industrial and Infrastructure
Development Corporation (KSIIDC) in 199.9 for developing the Greenfield Airport also did not have
any clause on closing down of HAL Airport for commercial operations, after the proposed
Greenfield airport was opened. Shareholders’ Agreement, 2002  also did not mention about this.
Hence the closing of HAL Airport is in violation of the very MoU which has envisaged the
Greenfield Airport project near Bengaluru.
31.3.2 The Committee was informed that many viability enhancement methods provided in the
procedure guideline to set up Greenfield Airports have been suggested including giving land on
concessional price, exempting taxes etc. But these methods do not envisage closure of existing
airport as a method to enhance the economical viability of a Greenfield airport project.
31.3.3 The Committee notes that the closure of HAL Airport was not mentioned in the
tender for Bengaluru Greenfield Airport. Naturally, all the parties who participated in the
tender process would have made their offers on this basis only. Making an offer of Closure
of HAL Airport, after the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT), appears to be a clear violation of
the due process.
31.3.4 As regards the restriction on having another airport within 150 Kms of existing
airport, granting permission to start a new Greenfield airport within that radium prima facie
seems to be in violation of the Government policy on airport infrastructure.
31.3.5 The pronounced policy also states that if an airport was allowed within an aerial
distance of 150 kms of an existing airport, a passenger sharing formula has to be evolved.
In the present case, the Government not only allowed the new airports to come up within
a distance of 150 kms but also closed down the existing profit-making airports, not to speak
of passenger sharing formula.
31.3.6 The Committee notes some merit in these arguments made by the representatives
of AAEU. It also feels that the closure of old airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad appears
to have been done in haste. It is no doubt deprives the AAI a good amount of revenue that
it needs to cross-subsidize airports in remote areas.
31.4 Concession Agreement - Irregularities
31.4.1 V arious arguments questioning the validity of the Concession Agreement signed between the
private companies and the Government were made before the Committee. For example, the
Concession Agreement (CA) dated 5th July, 2004 has a clause making it obligatory on GoI to
publish a notification declaring that HAL Airport will not be available for commercial civil aviation
from the date of opening of the new BIAL Airport at Devanahalli, Bengaluru.
31.4.2 The representatives of AAEU claimed that the Concession Agreement which was initially
prepared and approved by the Cabinet did not provide for the closure of HAL Airport. However,
allegedly, the clause related to HAL Airport closure was brought at a later stage into the
Concessional Agreement, after a demand made to this effect by the BIAL.

10
31.4.3 The Committee’s attention was drawn to a Notification issued by Government of India on
the 16th May, 2008 for HAL Airport which inter alia stated that in exercise of powers conferred
by Section 5A of the Aircraft Act, 1934, read with Rules 11 and 78 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937
and in deference of the contractual commitments including Clause 5.5 of the Concession Agreement
signed between Government of India and BIAL on the 5th July, 2004 and consequent on
commissioning of the Bengaluru International Airport at Devanahalli, w.e.f. 0001 hours of
23rd May, 2008, the HAL Airport at Bengaluru will no longer be available for “commercial civil
aviation operations”.
31.4.5 The representatives of AAEU pointed out that the powers under Section 5A are limited to
the matters mentioned in Section 5 and can be used only in two situations (a) if the security of
India is in danger and (b) if the safety of the Aircraft is in danger. In the given case of HAL
Airport, both these reasons are not present. Moreover, GoI itself says in the Notification that it has
used these powers “in deference of the contractual commitments including Clause 5.5 of the
Concession Agreement”, which clearly shows that the use of the powers u/s 5A was not due to
the above said reason but only in deference to the reasons best know to the Ministry and perhaps
to BIAL also.
31.4.6 They further argued that though the Notification says about closing HAL Airport for
“Commercial civil aviation operations” such a phrase is not defined in any of the Acts or rules
applicable in India (Aircraft Act 1934, Aircraft Rules 1937, Civil Aviation Requirements (CAR)).
31.5 Impossibility of the implementation of the Notification
31.5.1 With regard to the above notification, the representatives of AAl submitted that its
implementation is not possible. They stated that at HAL Airport Air Traffic Control (ATC) controls
almost half of the Bengaluru airspace even after the commissioning of BIAL. HAL ATC is an integral
part of Bengaluru HAL Airport. Even for the operations of BIAL Airport, HAL ATC operations are
necessary. HAL A TC still controls and will continue to control all aircraft operations including
commercial operations through the part of Bengaluru airspace controlled by it. Hence, it is a myth
that by this notification, commercial civil aviation operations of HAL Airport has been banned.
31.5.2 Even after the notification HAL Airport is being used by all types of Chartered Aircrafts.
Both parties to the Notification have already violated the notification by express action. BIAL has
violated the notification by giving permission to air taxi operations of M/s Deccan Aviation Limited
and Global Vectra Helicorp from and to HAL Airport. GoI has also violated when it has informed
Deccan Aviation that they do not have any objection for air taxi operations out of HAL Airport as
BIAL has no objection.
31.5.3 The Committee notes that commercial civil aviation activities are continuing in the
Bengaluru HAL Airport with the consent of the management of BIAL and Government of
India, whereas the Concession Agreement and the notification issued by the Government of
India clearly prohibits any commercial aviation activity. This shows that if the Government
wants, they can operationalise the old airports notwithstanding the Concession Agreement.
The Committee is of the considered view that HAL Airport at Bengaluru and Begumpet
Airport at Hyderabad may be made operational for domestic civil aviation.
31.5.4 The Committee notes that the Government has taken shelter of Section 5A of
Aircraft Act 1934 to close down HAL airport. However, Section 5A talks of closing of any
airport when there is danger to the aircraft/country. The above reason is totally irrelevant
for the instant case. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should
revisit various provision of the Concession Agreement to ensure that all the illegalities, etc.
are removed from it that are creating all kind of misgivings in the people’s mind.

11
31.6 NOC for setting up of Bengaluru Greenfield Airport by Ministry of Defence
31.6.1 It was contended before the Committee that as per the Aircraft Rules, 1937 and CAR, NOC
by the Ministry of Defence is mandatory for setting up of an airport. Ministry of Defence has
given its NOC for Devanahalli Greenfield Airport vide its letter No. 3(48)/02/D (Air. II) dated
03.03.04. But this NOC was subject to a condition that the operations at HAL Airport, Bengaluru
will continue even after the BIAL becomes functional and the choice of airport to be utilized should
be left to the operators/commuters/general public.
31.6.2 On the same ground, the license given to BIAL for airport operations by DGCA as per the
Aircraft Rules, 1937 (Rule 78) also becomes subject to this conditional NOC given by Ministry of
Defence. In view of this, they argued, GoI Notification for closing of HAL airport as well as
Aerodrome License of BIAL issued by DGCA ipso facto became null and void.
31.6.3 The Committee notes that the NOC for setting up of Bengaluru Greenfield Airport
by Ministry of Defence made it amply clear that the operations at HAL Airport Bengaluru
will continue even after the BIAL becomes functional and the choice of airport to be utilized
should be left to the operators/commuters/general public. Same is true about the license
issued to BIAL by the Director-General, Civil Aviation. In terms of Notification dated the
16th May, 2008, the HAL Airport stands closed for commercial operations. However, it is
still being used for chartered flights, air taxi services and VIP flights. The Committee fails
to understand that in such a situation, how the losses being incurred by the HAL Airport
would be compensated as desired by the Ministry of Defence while issuing NOC for the new
airport at Bengaluru.
31.7 Licensing of Airports
31.7.1 As per the Aircraft Rules 1937 (Rule 78) and also Civil Aviation Requirements (CAR)
aerodromes can be licensed either for public use that will be available to all persons on equal terms
and conditions or for Private Use  by the licensee and by individuals specifically authorized by the
licensee. It may be noted that private use of aerodromes exclude the operation of schedule flights
therefrom.
31.7.2 Their argument was that as per the above provisions of relevant rules and CAR, an
Aerodrome can be either for public use or private use only. There cannot be a third category, “for
public use but not for commercial civil aviation operations” as has been exactly done by the
notification about closer of the HAL Airport. It is thus clear that an aerodrome which is for public
use should be available to all persons on equal terms and conditions. Hence, an aerodrome like HAL
Airport, which is available for public use cannot be, closed for commercial civil aviation operations
and no such restriction can be imposed on an Airport for public use it was contended.
31.7.3 The Committee would like to have Ministry’s response on this point.
31.8 Similar International Examples
31.8.1 The Committee has learnt that Don Mueang International Airport (Old Bangkok Airport) was
closed completely on opening of new Suvarnabhumi Airport on 28.09.06, which was 40 kms away
from the city. However, mainly due to demands of low cost carriers and the higher costs at the new
Airport, old airport was reopened on 24.03.2007, without restrictions on distance or aircraft capacity.
31.8.2 Another example brought to the notice of the Committee was Dallas Love Field Airport
(USA) that was closed after new DFW International Airport become operational. There was no
Concession Agreement between the Operator and the Regulator or the Federal Government.
However, Southwest Airlines was permitted to operate from the old Airport even after opening of
DFW International Airport, as it was not a signatory to this Agreement.

12
31.8.3 The Committee takes note of these examples of more than one airport co-existing
in the cities to cater to the needs of various types of passenger requirements. The
Committee feels that the same can be applied in case of Bengaluru and Hyderabad Airports
also and the old airports in these cities may be made functional.
31.9 Role of AAI
31.9.1 It was further argued that AAI was an authority created by an Act of Parliament (55 of
1994) with no budgetary support and it was continuously making profit since inception and has
a Mini-ratna Status. The Airports Authority of India operates 127 airports including 16 international
airports, 83 domestic and 28 civil enclaves at defence airfields. AAI thus control and manages the
entire Indian airspace of 2.8 million square nautical miles. AAI provide communication navigation
and surveillance (CNS-ATM) services at all the airports in the country, including Greenfield
Airports. AAl’s competency in airport infrastructure is well known. AAI has constructed many
airports and has consulting projects in other countries like South Yemen, Libya, Algeria, Nauru,
Seychelles and Afghanistan.
31.10 Impact on AAI
31.10.1 The Committee was informed that due to the closure of HAL Airport alone, the estimated
revenue loss to AAI was around Rs 389 crores in 2007-08. Similarly, due to the closure of
Begumpet airport, Airports Authority of India lost and estimated revenue of Rs.221.15 crore during
this period. Thus, it lost of Rs.610 crore in the year 2007-08.
31.10.2 In addition to the above losses, AAI was losing revenue on account of RNFC (Route
Navigational Facility Charges) in other AAI Airports by cancellation of outbound flights from BIAL
Airport to other AAI Airports all over the country. It was underlined that AAI was running airports
in non-profit remote areas of the country as National obligations.
31.10.3 The Committee notes most  of the reasons advanced for the opening of the HAL
Airport at Bengaluru are applicable to  the Begumpet airport in Hyderabad also.
31.10.4 The committee notes that the equity contribution of the consortium of private
companies in BIAL is only Rs. 240/- crores. The rest of the financing has come from state
support, AAI, Government of Karnataka and by way of debt from financial institutions. The
land was also given on a concessional rate. The same is the case with HIAL also. The equity
contribution of the private companies is around Rs. 330/-  crores. The rest of the finance has
come from Government agencies and by way of debt from financial institutions. The
Committee notes that with the kind of resources and expertise that the Airports Authority
of India has, these airports could have been easily developed and operated by the Airports
Authority of India itself.
31.10.5 The Committee is, therefore, of the view that being leading airport infrastructure
provider, the Airports Authority of India which has got the resources and expertise should
have a better say in the modernization of airports in the country. The Committee
recommends that any future Greenfield airports or Brownfield airports project must be done
under the management of Airport Authority of India. JVCs can be formulated but the
Airports Authority of India must have a majority holding in the company and management
control must rest with it.

43. The issue of differential sales tax on ATF in this country and the resulting problem faced by
airline operators has engaged the attention of the Committee. Airline operators pointed out about the
financial losses due to the problem of ‘fuel ferrying’ or transiting. This issue has now become more
relevant in the context of current crisis faced by airlines that is largely attributed to high cost
of ATF. With regard to the problem of high price of ATF, the Committee reiterates its earlier
recommendation in its 138 report which inter-alia stated that –
“The Committee while appreciating the steps taken by the State Governments of
Kerala and Andhra Pradesh in reducing the Sales Tax on ATF from 32% to 4%
recommends that the Ministry pursue this long standing issue with other State

17
Governments so that uniformity of tax on ATF can be maintained. Since the cost of
fuel is an important component of cost structure, reduction in taxes on ATF will
definitely have a positive impact on the airfares. The Committee once again
recommends that Ministry of Finance should sympathetically consider and give
approval to the proposal of Ministry of Civil Aviation regarding notifying ATF as
‘Declared Good’ under Section 14 of Central Sales Tax Act on priority basis to all
the aircrafts so that sales tax on ATF could be contained within the maximum rate
of 4 per cent. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Finance may
also discuss the issue with the State Governments and try to persuade them to
reduce the sales tax on ATF. The Committee is of the opinion that the success of the
concept of low cost carrier mainly depends on the taxation of ATF which is very
much on the higher side. The Committee feels that reduction in airfares will bring
more new passengers to the airports.”

same terms and conditions of employment. Functional clause 12 covers all the services of
operations as well as non-operations. The JVC company has no constitutional right to send for an
option to get absorbed in the said JVC company since such provisions are not incorporated in the
AAI Act, 1994. The Principal employer (AAI) have extended 26% share value in the said agreement
by extending A TC/CNS services to the JVC company and parting away the other employees not
to discharge their duties at the respective airport is violation of the functional clause of Section 12
of the Act. Thus OMDA is a violation of clause 18 and manipulation of Functional clause 12 of
AAI Act 1994. Hence, the separating CNS/ATC with other areas of services is discriminatory.

allowed to continue their employment at the same station of posting as per the contract of service
issued on the date of appointment by AAI without altering any service conditions by the Principal

employees from one employer to another, as such the OMDA executed is not binding upon the
employees. No agreement (namely OMDA/concession agreement) can supersede the provisions of
a Parliament, Act. Hence the employees should continue to discharge their duties as long as the
leasing period continues with the AAI or terminates which ever is earlier. Therefore, it is stated
that suitable arrangement/provisions be made to accommodate all these employees at their
respective places of work. It may be mentioned that the said arrangement has been made with
regard to the privatization of Delhi Vidyut Board wherein the employees of the organization have
been retained in BSES on the same terms of employees enjoyed by them prior to privatization. The
various areas of violations are enumerated as below:
(a) Non-recognisition of various staff welfare committees by the Private Operator.
(b) Depriving the facility of AAI staff canteen, Mumbai Airport.
(c) Non-representation of staff in sports activities.
(d) Depriving staff of training facilities.
(e) Parking facility for the employees of Airports Authority of India. Earlier there was
specified parking lot for the employees
(f) The employees of AAI have been removed from the job which they were carrying out

modernization task of Mumbai and Delhi airports to the Joint Venture Company was to
complete it within the given time limit. However, the Committee feels that JVC has not
been able to meet the time frame as mentioned in the agreement to complete various
modernization projects (mandatory projects) and such projects are running behind schedule.

to avoid delays and cost over runs in the execution of the projects at Mumbai and Delhi
airports.

to the notice of the Committee. This type of behavior does not go well with the tourists and
creates an unpleasant atmosphere. The Committee desires that officials deputed at the
airport, should strictly be asked to be courteous and polite with the passengers particularly,
the tourist from other countries. The officials deputed at the airport and dealing with the
passengers/tourists should be more careful, polite, helpful and tourist friendly.

regular interaction among various stakeholders of Chattrapati Shivaji International Airport

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
BENGALURU INTERNATIONAL AIRPOR T LIMITED (BIAL) AND HYDERABAD
INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT LIMITED (HIAL)
The Committee found the plan and design of the Greenfield airports to be of the
international standard with certain useful facilities for the comfort and convenience of the

and quick immigration clearance, large number of shops, eateries, etc. However, the
Committee also came across certain areas that needed immediate attention. For example,
the Committee found, that the passengers at the Greenfield airports have to pay
exorbitant prices for food items. The eateries are charging much more than the MRP,
which is against the Supreme Court order. There is no separate canteen for the
employees and the staff working at the airports. The drivers and others who are waiting
outside the airports have no affordable canteen facility and basic amenities like toilets
and bathrooms. The Committee recommends that the Government should ensure that the
Greenfield Airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad provide basic facilities to the drivers and
passengers and stop the eateries from charging exorbitant prices. Private airlines have to
cough up hefty amounts for parking bays and aerobridges, security charges, lounge
rentals, telephone rentals and other facilities at the new airports. (Para 13)
The parking charges for vehicles are also quite heavy at the new airports. At
Bengaluru, it is Rs.40/- per hour and Rs.20/-per additional hours. The Committee is
surprised to know that at Hyderabad airport, a vehicle while entering the airport for
dropping or picking up a passenger has to pay Rs.35/- per trip. The Committee notes that
space earmarked for passenger seating areas was inadequate and numbers of seats are
also not adequate, causing inconvenience to the passengers during peak times. This is so
because much of the airport space has been let out for commercial use and given to
shopping outlets and F&B outlets. There is conspicuous absence of lounges at these
airports. There is a need for creation of additional reserved lounge for VIPs and
passengers. To help and guide the passengers at these airports, there should be round-the-
clock help service at these airports. There were inadequate facilities provided for free
drinking water at these airports. More drinking water fountains should be installed. The
emergency medical facilities for treatment of the passengers in case of sudden illness
should be in place in all the new airports as has been done at the new Hyderabad airport.
(Para 14)
The Committee recommends that the flight delay or cancellation must be reported
to passengers well in time to avoid hardships to the passengers. The baggage handling
process should be strengthened so as to reduce the baggage delivery time and hardship
to the passengers. Apron driving discipline should be maintained to avoid any accident on
apron and staff should be given proper training for the driving skills and behaviors. There
should be integration of air and ground surveillance information along with flight related
data to enhance air travel safety and efficient air traffic management. (Para 15)
The private operators should recognize various staff welfare Committees of Airports
Authority of India and others working at these airports. There should be regular
consultative and coordination meeting of all the stakeholders at the new airports so as to
resolve the different issues/grievances. (Para 16)

The Committee learnt that it was discouraging for the short-haul passengers to
take air travel after the new airports. A higher User Development Fee (UDF) was being
charged by the new airport developers from the passengers. The user development fee
added with high taxi/bus fares due to long distances, compel the passengers to use other
means of transport such as road and, trains for the short distance destinations. This has,
in fact rendered the air travel from these airports added with high ATF prices, just
prohibitive. (Para 17)

2006) had recommended that the users should not be burdened with ADF/UDF for

objective to make civil aviation a mass, rather than an elitist model of travel and to

recommendation of the Task Force the Committee feels that the imposition of UDF on
passengers is a retrograde step contravening the Task Force recommendations and

more UDF may be imposed on passengers in any of the airports. (Para 18)

The Committee notes that the Government of India appears to be unconcerned
about the obligation of BIAL to construct and provide an airport as per the concession
agreement. Even the area and capacity were not verified before permitting to open new
and closing HAL Airport. This appears to be an irregularity committed by Government of
India in this matter. (Para 19.6)
The Committee notes that hundreds of crores of rupees were spent for developing
infrastructure at the old airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad but it is lying unutilized
due to the closure of airports for commercial purposes. Another interesting thing brought
to the notice of the Committee is that the old airports, the HAL Airport and Begumpet
Airport, are being used for operation of VIP flights, Non-schedule Flights, General
Aviation, Helicopter-Taxis, etc. During the deliberations of the Committee the Airports
Authority of India reported that there is absolutely no problem in opening up two airports
simultaneously in a city. The Committee therefore, recommends that the old airports of
Hyderabad and Bengaluru may be used exclusively for short haul flights which are

vendors, taxi drivers, auto drivers, loaders etc. Despite the assurances given by the BIAL
and HIAL managements, they have not been accommodated in the new airports. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that all those people who are directly or indirectly
affected due to closure of the HAL Airport and Begumpet Airport may be given preference
and suitably accommodated at the new Green Field Airports. (Para 25)
The Committee is of the opinion that the HAL Airport is most convenient for
common public due to it being situated closer to the City Centre, easy accessibility and
availability of multi-mode transport options like Bus, Auto, Taxis, even 2-wheeler, etc.
HAL Airport, therefore, would be more convenient and economical for public compared to
BIAL due to absence of UDF and less transportation cost due to multiple modes and
shorter distance. Less time in coming and going from the airport is also important aspect
in this regard. (Para 26)

The Committee further recommends that the old airports may be made operational
for short-haul passengers. Moreover, this is the practice being followed in many of the
major cities in the world wherein more than one airport exists. There is no reason or
justification for keeping the hundreds of crores of worth infrastructure at the old airports
idle just to be used for VIP and other flights. (Para 27)
CLOSURE OF HAL AND BEGUMPET AIRPORTS—SOME LEGAL AND PROCEDURAL ISSUES
The Committee notes that the closure of HAL Airport was not mentioned in the
tender for Bengaluru Greenfield Airport. Naturally, all the parties who participated in the
tender process would have made their offers on this basis only. Making an offer of
Closure of HAL Airport, after the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT), appears to be a clear
violation of the due process. (Para 31.3.3)
As regards the restriction on having another airport within 150 kms of existing
airport, granting permission to start a new Greenfield airport within that radium prima
facie  seems to be in violation of the Government policy on airport infrastructure.
(Para 31.3.4)
The pronounced policy also states that if an airport was allowed within an aerial
distance of 150 kms of an existing airport, a passenger sharing formula has to be evolved.
In the present case, the Government not only allowed the new airports to come up within
a distance of 150 kms but also closed down the existing profit-making airports, not to
speak of passenger sharing formula. (Para 31.3.5)
The Committee notes some merit in these arguments made by the representatives
of AAEU. It also feels that the closure of old airports at Bengaluru and Hyderabad
appears to have been done in haste. It is no doubt deprives the AAI a good amount of
revenue that it needs to cross-subsidize airports in remote areas. (Para 31.3.6)

IMPOSSIBILITY OF THE IMPLEMENTATION OF THE NOTIFICATION
The Committee notes that commercial civil aviation activities are continuing in the
Bengaluru HAL Airport with the consent of the management of BIAL and Government of
India, whereas the Concession Agreement and the notification issued by the Government
of India clearly prohibits any commercial aviation activity. This shows that if the
Government wants, they can operationalise the old airports notwithstanding the
Concession Agreement. The Committee is of the considered view that HAL Airport at

Aircraft Act 1934 to close down HAL airport. However, Section 5A talks of closing of any
airport when there is danger to the aircraft/country. The above reason is totally irrelevant

revisit various provision of the Concession Agreement to ensure that all the illegalities,
etc. are removed from it that are creating all kind of misgivings in the people’s mind.

above the MRP, lack of basic amenities/canteen facilities, higher charges towards security,
lounge rental, aviation services, parking, telephone and other facilities, no residential
space for the ATC staff, no co-ordination with the user agencies and airport operators, no
round the clock help service available; delay in execution of building projects at Mumbai
and Delhi, inadequate inter-terminal passenger transportation facilities and airlines were
not finding space for parking bays in the airport terminal and charges for this were very
high. (Para 59)
The Committee observes that due to lack of adequate civic utilities like toilets,
drinking water fountains etc. outside arrival/departure hall of all the four airport,
passengers/tourists experienced difficulties. There was also lack of toilet facility at car/taxi
parking area outside the Airports. The Committee observes that Airport Operators should
not ignore the needs of such people. The Committee recommends that toilet and drinking
water facilities should be provided outside the arrival/departure lounge and parking areas
in order to avoid inconvenience to the passengers and co-passengers. (Para 60)
Some instances of impolite behavior with the passengers at the airports was
brought to the notice of the Committee. This type of behavior does not go well with the
tourists and creates an unpleasant atmosphere. The Committee desires that officials

28
deputed at the airport, should strictly be asked to be courteous and polite with the
passengers particularly, the tourist from other countries. The officials deputed at the
airport and dealing with the passengers/tourists should be more careful, polite, helpful and
tourist friendly. (Para 61)
The Committee recommends that a coordination mechanism may be evolved for
regular interaction among various stakeholders of Chattrapati Shivaji International
Airport with representation from agencies such as MIAL, Airports Authority of India,
Employees Unions of Airports Authority of India, various airlines etc. This mechanism will
iron out differences among the stakeholders of the Airport and will enable smooth
functioning of the airport. (Para 62)
The Committee, after visiting the airports at Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and
Hyderabad and after considering the facts and information made available to it in respect
of modernization and development of private airports as well as closure of HAL and
Begumpet airports, has gained impression that had all the processes and procedures been
done in far more transparent and acceptable manner, most of the objections and
controversies could have been avoided. Right from arranging finances for participating
joint venture companies, giving thousands acres of land on concessional rates and allowing
them to use the land commercially, signing OMDA and Concession Agreements favorable
to JVCs and closure of existing airports, etc. are some of the areas about which there
are lot of misgivings in the minds of people and media keeps writing about these.
(Para 63)
Besides, the Airports Authority of India, advertently or inadvertently, appears to
not being given its due. Even though, ATC operations of all the airports are still with
them, the closure of HAL and Begumpet airports and placing Airports Authority of India
virtually at the mercy of the management of private airports, speaks a lot about it. The
manner in which the Concession Agreement and OMDA were signed has also invited wide
criticism and these are alleged to have violated the existing policies, guidelines, norms,
rules, etc. The Committee feels that there appears to be some truth in the apprehensions
that are being raised against the Government in the entire exercise of privatizing the
airports, developing the Greenfield airports and the related matters. The Committee
expects that the Government of the day to provide convincing explanation to all the
points, raised in this report to clear the apprehensions that are being flown thick and
wide. It is for the Government to clarify the entire matter. (Para 64)
The Committee hastens to point out that it had sought to know the Government's
response to the various points brought to its notice vide a letter dated 3rd October, 2008.
Despite reminders, the Committee had not received the response of the Government till
the time the Committee’s report was adopted on the 20th October, 2008. (Para 65)
